description: Thallium is a silvery-white post-transition metal with atomic number 81 that is not found free in nature. When isolated, it resembles tin but discolors when exposed to air. It was discovered independently by William Crookes and Claude-Auguste Lamy in 1861 using flame spectroscopy, and the name derives from the Greek word for "green shoot" due to its characteristic green spectral line.
uses: Approximately 65% of thallium production is used in the electronics industry, with the remainder used in the pharmaceutical industry and glass manufacturing. It is also used in infrared detectors. The radioisotope thallium-201 is used in small amounts in nuclear medicine scans during cardiac stress tests. Soluble thallium salts were historically used in rat poisons and insecticides, though these uses have been restricted or banned in many countries due to toxicity.
characteristics: Thallium is a soft, highly electrically conducting metal with a low melting point of 304°C and is malleable and sectile enough to be cut with a knife. It has a metallic luster that quickly tarnishes to a bluish-gray tinge when exposed to air, and a heavy layer of oxide builds up on the metal if left in air. Thallium reacts with water to form thallium hydroxide and tends to form +3 and +1 oxidation states, with the +1 state being far more prominent in thallium than in other group 13 elements.
